folder.clickHint: Click a device to work on it.
folder.clickHintText: A node counts as a device as soon as a template matches it — below that nothing is searched. Where none matches, the node still appears in the list as soon as it has datapoints of its own.
folder.nothingHere: There is nothing here that could become a device.
guess.hint: Fills the pattern’s free slots from the remaining datapoints — an attempt, not knowledge. Guessed by name, value list, unit and type; every assignment is marked “guessed” and can be discarded one by one.
guess.locked: {0}× guessed, still undecided — keep (✓) or discard (✕) first, then creating and saving unlock.
guess.none: Nothing to suggest: either every slot is taken, or no remaining datapoint fits a free slot.
guess.tplAsk: This device is identified as “{0}”, so the assignment is already settled. The suggestion guesses additional slots from the remaining data points — an attempt, not knowledge, and every match would need checking. Meant for special cases, e.g. when the device can do more than the template covers.
guess.tplHint: The template already covers this device — guessing here is for special cases only.
guess.tplTitle: Suggest free slots despite a template?
help.aliases: Pick an existing alias on the left. Remove points, change roles, sources and formulas — or move, rename and delete it.
help.aliasesAdd: To add points to an alias, the way via “to the source →” (top right, next to the alias name) is easier: the template applies there, and every data point of the device is offered with a ready role — here you would have to enter each one by hand.
help.sources: Pick a device or channel on the left. The workbench recognises what it is and proposes a finished alias. If one already exists, it is updated instead.
help.templates: Pick a template on the left. Bundled ones can be viewed and duplicated, your own edited. The trial run shows which devices it matches.
info.explain: work perfectly normally and stay where you created them. Nothing extra is written — the alias stays as it is. They simply are not part of what ioBroker considers a {0}; their role does not fit any of its slots. It only starts to matter once you hand the alias to Alexa, Google Home or a device UI: those will see a {0} without these points. In VIS, in scripts and in history you use them like any other datapoint.
leave.body: There are changes on {0} that have not been written yet. Switching now discards them.
leave.title: Unsaved changes
list.onlyPatternHint: Checks exactly the points that get a slot in the chosen pattern — everything else is unchecked and not created.
list.otherSourceHint: This point does not read from {0} but from {1}.
list.resetHint: Discards every change made here — checkboxes, roles, formulas, sources — and shows the state as stored again.
list.tplHint: Checks exactly the points the template proposes — regardless of what the alias holds today.
move.done: Moved. The alias is now at {0}.
move.exists: {0} already exists. Remove it first or pick another name.
move.nested: The target sits below the alias itself (or the other way round). Moving would delete its own parent node — please pick a place beside it.
move.noScripts: The ID does not appear in any script.
move.scriptsHead1: One script mentions the old ID:
move.title: Move alias
move.unchanged: Folder and name unchanged — nothing to do.
move.warnHistory: Only the setting that recording is enabled moves along. From now on a new, empty series starts under the new ID. Everything recorded so far stays in the database under the old ID — it is not lost, but it will no longer be extended. Charts and Grafana queries pointing at the old ID receive nothing new; pointed at the new one, they lack the history.
move.warnHistoryHead: Recorded values do not move along.
move.warnRefs: vis views, Alexa and Google names and other adapters cannot be inspected. Anything pointing at the old ID must be adjusted by hand.
move.warnRefsHead: What else refers to the old ID.
mq.ask: Ask the device for its commands
mq.askHint: This is a plain query — it switches nothing and changes no setting.
mq.askNoAnswer: No answer. Either the device is offline, or it listens on a different topic.
mq.doneHint: Detection runs again in a moment — a template that did not match before can match now.
mq.instantHintOff: Without SetOption59 an alias reading from tele/STATE shows the old value for minutes after switching. Enabling is a persistent setting on the device — it switches nothing and only changes how often the device reports.
mq.instantHintOn: SetOption59 is set: the device reports every change at once, not only with the next telemetry. Measured at three seconds.
mq.instantHintUnknown: The device has not been asked yet. "Ask" sends an empty query to SetOption59 — it changes nothing.
mq.intro: Not every Tasmota is set up the same way. A missing or mute point is not a fault in itself — it only matters once an alias is meant to switch through it, or a template needs it for detection.
mq.neverReported: The device has not fully reported since it started, so its command list is unknown.
mq.nothingYet: The device has not sent anything yet that commands could be read from.
mq.onlyResult: So far only the reply to a single command arrived, not the whole state — the list may be incomplete.
mq.repairHint: These points exist but are not allowed to send. An alias switching through them does nothing, and nothing about it shows.
mq.title: MQTT device
pattern.label: Pattern
pattern.noPlaceLegend: Rows shaded like this have no slot in the {0} pattern
pattern.noPlaceLong: no slot in the {0} pattern — the point is still created and fully usable, only Alexa and friends count it separately
pattern.slotName: This point sits in slot "{0}" of the {1} pattern. Slot names come from the type-detector and are the same everywhere — they are not translated, because the alias datapoint is named exactly that.
pattern.typeMismatch: Slot {0} requires {1}, but {2} is set — the state drops out of the pattern even though the role is right.
result.channelsHint: This device has {0} channels that make sense on their own. Choose below: one alias for all of it, or one per channel.
result.extraSwitches: Included: {0} points from other channels that the {1} pattern has no slot for. They are created, but do not count as the device’s switch or feedback. For separate control, use "one device per channel" below.
result.header: What the type-detector makes of it
result.sourceCountHint: The points of this alias read from more than one node. "to the source" leads to the one most of them come from; a click shows all of them.
result.toAliasHint: Jumps to the alias built from this device.
result.toSourceHint: Jumps to the device this alias was built from. Templates only apply there — in alias mode an alias can be maintained, but not rebuilt from a template.
result.tooManyStates: That would be a device with {0} states — usually this means the wrong node is selected. In the tree on the left, nodes that look like a single device carry a dot. You can still build it this way.
swap.done: Swapped. The alias now reads from {0}.
swap.gone: This device no longer exists — which is exactly what this is for.
swap.guessHint: Rows marked “guessed” were matched by name or role — please check those individually.
swap.keeps: The alias keeps its id, names, roles and formulas, its history in the database and its room and function. Only where each point reads from and writes to changes.
swap.mindHint: The alias formulas stay as they are — if the new source scales differently, the values will be wrong afterwards. The formula sits in the point's detail row.
swap.noWriteMatch: no write target found — this point will not write anywhere
swap.same: That is the same source as before.

tpls.multipleHelp: The {0} in the paths is replaced by %N% — only at the end of a segment, so ENERGY.Power stays intact.
tpls.multipleNoNumber: Enter which number in the paths is the output. Without it the template stays a single one.
tpls.multipleOff: A device with POWER1, POWER2 … becomes a folder with one channel per output.
